questions.context: Multi-region infrastructure failover coordinator
questions.stem: A coordinator agent responds to cloud region outages by dispatching to per-region 'health-check' subagents and, if a region is confirmed down, a 'traffic-reroute' subagent. It was built with a fixed sequence: check all 4 regions in a hardcoded order, then always invoke traffic-reroute once at the end, regardless of how many (if any) regions were actually found unhealthy. During a recent single-region blip that self-resolved in 30 seconds, the coordinator still finished its full 4-region check and then rerouted traffic anyway, causing an unnecessary and disruptive reroute for a region that was never actually down. What orchestration change most directly fixes this?

choices.text: Keep the fixed sequence of checking all 4 regions before ever rerouting, but shorten each health-check subagent's timeout so the whole sequence completes faster, reducing the window in which a self-resolving blip could be caught mid-check.

Configure the coordinator's AgentDefinition with a `failoverPlan.autoElect: true` option so the SDK automatically determines, without the coordinator's own reasoning, whether a detected outage is transient enough to skip the reroute step.

Keep invoking traffic-reroute unconditionally after every check cycle, but have the traffic-reroute subagent itself check whether any region was actually flagged unhealthy and silently no-op if none were, so the reroute call is harmless when unnecessary.

Have the coordinator act on each health-check subagent's result as it comes back, and only invoke traffic-reroute for regions actually confirmed unhealthy at that point — including skipping the reroute step entirely if every region checks out healthy — rather than always running the full fixed sequence and rerouting unconditionally at the end.

questions.explanationEn: Acting on each health-check result as it arrives and rerouting only for regions genuinely confirmed unhealthy — including skipping the reroute step entirely when everything checks out — directly fixes the problem: the coordinator's routing now reflects reality instead of running an unconditional sequence regardless of findings. Shortening the timeout only shrinks the window for this specific failure without addressing the actual cause — an unconditional reroute step invoked regardless of findings — so a self-resolving blip that happens to outlast even a shorter timeout would still trigger the same disruptive reroute. A fabricated `failoverPlan.autoElect` option isn't a real AgentDefinition field, and delegating the transience judgment to an unspecified automatic mechanism removes the coordinator's own visibility into and control over the decision, which the actual fix keeps front and center. Having traffic-reroute itself silently no-op when unnecessary still invokes the subagent every cycle unconditionally, spending the call and adding a layer of self-suppression logic instead of the coordinator simply not calling it when it isn't needed.
questions.explanationJa: 各ヘルスチェックサブエージェントの結果が返ってくるたびにそれに基づいて行動し、その時点で実際に不健全と確認されたリージョンに対してのみtraffic-rerouteを呼び出す(すべてのリージョンが正常であればリルート自体をまったく呼び出さない)ことが、findings(所見)にかかわらず固定シーケンスを実行し最後に無条件でリルートするのではなく、この問題を直接修正します。コーディネーターのルーティングが実際の状況を反映するようになります。タイムアウトを短くする方法は、この特定の失敗が起こる時間の窓を狭めるだけで、無条件で呼び出されるリルートステップという実際の原因には対応しておらず、短くしたタイムアウトよりも長く続く自己解消するブリップであれば同じ破壊的なリルートを依然として引き起こします。架空の`failoverPlan.autoElect`というオプションはAgentDefinitionの実在するフィールドではなく、一時的かどうかの判断を未規定の自動的な仕組みに委ねることは、実際の修正が中心に据えているコーディネーター自身の可視性と制御を奪ってしまいます。traffic-reroute自身が不要なときに黙ってno-opする方法も、依然として毎サイクル無条件にサブエージェントを呼び出しており、呼び出しのコストを払ったうえで自己抑制のロジックの層を追加しているだけで、コーディネーターが単に不要なときに呼び出さないという方法には及びません。

questions.context: Backward-compatibility and consumer-impact subagents auditing an API version bump
questions.stem: A coordinator running in Claude Code needs a 'backward-compatibility' subagent and a 'consumer-impact' subagent to each independently assess a proposed API v2 spec against the same v1 OpenAPI spec and the same list of known internal consumers of the API, without either seeing the other's conclusions first. The engineer invokes the backward-compatibility subagent with both documents attached to its Task prompt, then invokes the consumer-impact subagent with only the instruction 'review the API change we just discussed for consumer impact,' assuming it can see the same documents. The consumer-impact subagent then produces a generic, uninformative response because it has no actual spec or consumer list to work from. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Give the consumer-impact subagent its own complete, explicit Task prompt that independently includes the v1 spec, the proposed v2 spec, and the consumer list, the same way the backward-compatibility subagent's prompt does, since a subagent has no access to documents attached only to a different, earlier Task invocation.

Re-invoke the backward-compatibility subagent a second time and have it forward its own understanding of the specs and consumer list into the consumer-impact subagent's prompt as a summary, since the backward-compatibility subagent already has the documents loaded.

Attach the v1 spec, v2 spec, and consumer list to the coordinator's own system prompt instead of either subagent's Task prompt, since subagents inherit any document explicitly attached to the parent coordinator's system prompt via a field called `inheritsBreakingChangeContext`.

Keep the consumer-impact subagent's prompt as a short instruction referencing 'the API change we just discussed,' but increase the subagent's max_tokens so it has more room to reconstruct the missing context from the reference alone.

questions.explanationEn: Giving the consumer-impact subagent its own complete Task prompt with the v1 spec, v2 spec, and consumer list — independently, the same way the other subagent's prompt does — is correct because each Task invocation is its own isolated context with no access to a different invocation's attachments. Having the backward-compatibility subagent summarize the documents into the consumer-impact subagent's prompt would supply some data, but it also means the consumer-impact subagent's understanding is now filtered through the backward-compatibility subagent's own summary and framing rather than the original documents, and it also breaks the requirement that neither should see the other's conclusions first if that summary includes any of its own findings. There is no `inheritsBreakingChangeContext` field or any mechanism by which documents attached to a coordinator's system prompt automatically become available inside a subagent's isolated Task context — that inheritance path doesn't exist. Increasing max_tokens gives the subagent more room to produce a longer response, not more information to work from; a vague reference to 'the API change we just discussed' still resolves to nothing concrete in an isolated context regardless of how much output room the subagent has.
questions.explanationJa: consumer-impactサブエージェントに、backward-compatibilityサブエージェントのプロンプトと同じように、v1スペック・提案されたv2スペック・consumerリストを独立して含む完全なTaskプロンプトを与えることが正しい対応です。各Task呼び出しはそれぞれ独立したコンテキストであり、別の呼び出しに添付された文書にはアクセスできないためです。backward-compatibilityサブエージェントに文書を要約させてconsumer-impactサブエージェントのプロンプトに転送する方法は、いくらかのデータは提供しますが、consumer-impactサブエージェントの理解が元の文書ではなくbackward-compatibilityサブエージェント自身の要約とフレーミングを通してフィルタリングされたものになってしまい、その要約に自身の所見が含まれていれば、互いの結論を先に見るべきではないという要件にも違反します。`inheritsBreakingChangeContext`というフィールドや、コーディネーターのシステムプロンプトに添付された文書がサブエージェントの独立したTaskコンテキスト内で自動的に利用可能になる仕組みは存在せず、そのような継承経路はありません。max_tokensを増やすことはサブエージェントがより長いレスポンスを生成する余地を与えるだけで、参照できる情報が増えるわけではありません。『先ほど話し合ったAPIの変更』という漠然とした参照は、出力の余地がどれだけあっても独立したコンテキストの中では具体的な何にも結びつきません。

questions.context: Data-deletion agent required to confirm legal hold clearance before purging records
questions.stem: A data-deletion agent is instructed via its system prompt: 'Never call purge_user_records until legal_hold_status returns CLEARED for that user.' In an incident, the agent purged a user's records while a legal hold was still ACTIVE, because it reasoned that the hold 'appeared to be an administrative formality unrelated to the actual deletion request' and proceeded anyway. The team wants a fix that holds even against a future prompt injection (e.g., text in a deletion request trying to convince the model a hold doesn't really apply). What change most directly closes this gap?

choices.text: Strengthen the system prompt with an explicit example of this exact failure mode, instructing the model never to treat a legal hold as 'just a formality' regardless of how the deletion request is phrased.

Implement a PreToolUse hook on the purge_user_records tool that programmatically queries the actual legal_hold_status for that user and denies the tool call unless the returned value is exactly CLEARED, independent of any reasoning the model applies to the request.

Add a required boolean field named purgeConfirmed to the purge_user_records tool's input schema that the model must explicitly set to true, and trust the model to only set it once it has genuinely verified the hold is cleared.

Move the legal-hold check into a dedicated 'compliance-gatekeeper' subagent invoked immediately before every purge_user_records call, and have the coordinator trust that subagent's own textual conclusion about whether the hold is cleared.

questions.explanationEn: A PreToolUse hook that programmatically checks the actual legal_hold_status value and denies the call unless it is exactly CLEARED enforces the rule deterministically, outside of and prior to any model reasoning, so no amount of persuasive framing in the request — injected or not — can talk the loop around it. Adding a more specific example to the system prompt still leaves enforcement entirely inside the model's own reasoning, which is exactly the mechanism that failed when the hold was dismissed as 'just a formality.' A purgeConfirmed boolean the model itself must set still depends on the model's own judgment about whether the hold is genuinely cleared, so it inherits the same 'talked around by reasoning' weakness the team wants eliminated. Routing the check through a separate compliance-gatekeeper subagent still gates the call on another LLM's textual conclusion rather than a deterministic check against the actual status field, so it can be reasoned around the same way the original instruction was.
questions.explanationJa: PreToolUseフックを実装し、purge_user_recordsツールに対して該当ユーザーの実際のlegal_hold_statusをプログラム的に確認し、返された値が正確にCLEAREDでない限りツール呼び出しを拒否するようにすることで、モデルがリクエストに対してどのような推論を適用しようとも関係なく、決定的にルールを強制できます。この失敗の具体例をシステムプロンプトに追加して強化する方法は、依然として強制のすべてをモデル自身の推論の中に置いており、法的ホールドが『単なる形式的なもの』として却下された、まさにその仕組みのままです。モデル自身が設定しなければならないpurgeConfirmedというブール値も、ホールドが本当に解除されたかどうかについてのモデル自身の判断に依存したままであり、チームが排除したい『推論で言いくるめられる』という弱点を引き継ぎます。別の『compliance-gatekeeper』サブエージェントにチェックを移し、そのサブエージェント自身のテキストによる結論をコーディネーターが信頼する方法も、実際のステータスフィールドに対する決定的なチェックではなく別のLLMのテキスト推論によってゲートしているにすぎず、元の指示と同じように言いくるめられる可能性があります。

questions.context: Compliance audit-trail agent needing deterministic log-entry formatting
questions.stem: An agent that writes audit-trail entries via a `log_action` tool sometimes writes free-form descriptions ('reviewed and approved the request') and sometimes writes the required structured format ('ACTION=approve; ACTOR=agent; TARGET=request-4471'), inconsistently, despite explicit prompt instructions to always use the structured format. The compliance team needs every entry actually written to the audit log to be in the structured format, without depending on the model remembering the rule every time. Which Agent SDK mechanism directly and deterministically enforces this?

choices.text: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks any log_action call whose description isn't already in the structured format, forcing the model to retry indefinitely without the hook itself ever performing the reformatting, so a model that keeps writing free-form text loops until it hits the turn cap.

Set a `preNormalize: "audit-format"` option directly on the log_action tool definition, which causes the SDK to automatically rewrite the description argument into the structured format before the tool function ever receives it.

Register a PostToolUse hook on log_action that runs after every call, deterministically reformats whatever description was actually written into the required structured format, and corrects the log entry if the model's write didn't already match it — independent of whether the model remembered the format that turn.

Add a more detailed explanation of the required structured format to the log_action tool's description field, since tool descriptions are the primary signal the model uses to decide how to call a tool.

questions.explanationEn: A PostToolUse hook that runs after every log_action call and deterministically reformats the description that was actually written enforces the required structure regardless of whether the model remembered the rule that turn, because the correction happens outside of the model's own behavior. Blocking non-compliant writes with a PreToolUse hook and forcing indefinite retries is deterministic in that it rejects bad calls, but it never performs the correction itself, so a model that keeps producing free-form text simply loops until the turn cap rather than ever reaching a correctly formatted state. A `preNormalize` option that auto-rewrites arguments before the tool function runs is not a real SDK mechanism — no such automatic input-coercion configuration exists on tool definitions. A more detailed tool description can influence how the model chooses to phrase its calls, but it's still a prompt-level signal subject to the same turn-to-turn inconsistency described in the scenario, not a deterministic enforcement point.
questions.explanationJa: log_actionへのあらゆる呼び出しの後に実行されるPostToolUseフックを登録し、実際に書き込まれた説明文を必須の構造化フォーマットに決定的に再フォーマットする方法は、その回にモデルがルールを覚えていたかどうかに関係なく必須の構造を強制します。修正がモデル自身の挙動の外側で行われるためです。準拠していない書き込みをPreToolUseフックでブロックし無期限に再試行させる方法は、不正な呼び出しを拒否するという意味では決定的ですが、修正そのものは一切行わないため、自由形式のテキストを書き続けるモデルは正しくフォーマットされた状態に一度も到達することなくターン上限まで単にループし続けます。ツール関数が受け取る前に引数を自動的に書き換える`preNormalize`というオプションは実在するSDKの仕組みではなく、ツール定義にそのような自動的な入力変換の設定は存在しません。ツールのdescriptionフィールドに必須フォーマットのより詳細な説明を追加する方法は、モデルが呼び出しをどう表現するかに影響を与えうるという点ではもっともらしいですが、依然としてプロンプトレベルのシグナルであり、シナリオで説明されているターンごとの不整合と同じ弱点を抱えたままで、決定的な強制ポイントにはなりません。

questions.context: Automated dependency license-compatibility audit across a monorepo
questions.stem: A team asks Claude Code to audit license compatibility for every third-party dependency across a 40-package monorepo, flagging any package whose license is incompatible with the project's own MIT license. The current approach is a fixed, unconditional chain applied identically to every package: 'read package.json,' then 'look up the declared license,' then 'compare against an allow-list,' with no step ever considering findings from other packages. Most packages resolve cleanly this way, but a meaningful number of packages declare a license that's technically compatible in isolation yet becomes incompatible only in combination with a specific transitive dependency shared across multiple packages (a cross-package interaction the fixed per-package chain can't see), and a few packages have no machine-readable license field at all, requiring a different lookup path (checking the LICENSE file directly). What is the most correct fix to the task decomposition strategy?

choices.text: Keep the fixed per-package chain exactly as is, but add a uniform fourth step ('re-verify') applied identically to every package after the first three, on the theory that a uniform extra pass will catch both the cross-package conflicts and the missing-license-field cases equally well.

Configure the audit with a `licenseGraph.autoResolve: true` setting so Claude Code automatically detects and reconciles cross-package transitive license conflicts without needing an explicit adaptive tracking step in the task decomposition.

Abandon the per-package approach entirely and process all 40 packages' package.json files in one single pass by concatenating them into one very large prompt, so the model can see every declared license simultaneously and reason about cross-package interactions in one shot.

Keep the fixed per-package chain for the straightforward majority, but add a genuinely adaptive step that tracks which transitive dependencies are shared across packages to detect cross-package license conflicts the fixed chain can't see on its own, plus a separate fallback path for packages with no machine-readable license field that checks the LICENSE file directly instead of forcing the same rigid chain onto every package regardless of what data is actually available.

questions.explanationEn: Keeping the fixed chain for the straightforward majority while adding a genuinely adaptive step that tracks shared transitive dependencies (to catch cross-package conflicts) and a separate fallback path for packages lacking a machine-readable license field directly addresses both failure modes without forcing every package through an identical rigid chain, which is the core lesson about combining fixed chaining with adaptive, cross-item awareness where it's actually needed. Adding a uniform 're-verify' step to the same fixed, per-package chain doesn't introduce any cross-package awareness — a per-package re-verification still can't detect that two packages share a transitive dependency, nor does it change what to do for a package with no machine-readable license field. A fabricated `licenseGraph.autoResolve` setting implying Claude Code automatically handles cross-package conflict detection without any explicit decomposition step is not a real capability — the adaptive tracking step has to actually be part of the task's design, not assumed away by a configuration flag. Concatenating all 40 packages' files into one giant prompt abandons the working per-package approach for the majority of straightforward cases entirely, trading a targeted fix for a heavier, less reliable architecture that also risks exceeding practical context limits as the monorepo grows.
questions.explanationJa: 単純な大多数のパッケージには固定のチェーンを維持しつつ、共有される推移的依存関係を追跡してクロスパッケージのライセンス競合(固定チェーン単独では見えないもの)を検出する本当に適応的なステップと、機械可読なライセンスフィールドを持たないパッケージのためにLICENSEファイルを直接確認する別のフォールバック経路を追加することが、すべてのパッケージに同一の硬直したチェーンを強制するのではなく、両方の失敗モードに直接対応します。これは、固定チェーンと、本当に必要な箇所での適応的でクロスアイテムな認識を組み合わせるという核心的な教訓です。同じ固定のパッケージごとのチェーンに一律の『再検証』ステップを追加する方法は、クロスパッケージの認識をまったく導入しません。パッケージごとの再検証は、2つのパッケージが推移的依存関係を共有していることを検出できず、機械可読なライセンスフィールドを持たないパッケージに対して何をすべきかも変わりません。架空の`licenseGraph.autoResolve`という設定で、明示的な分解ステップなしにClaude Codeが自動的にクロスパッケージの競合検出を処理するという説明は実在する機能ではなく、適応的な追跡ステップはタスク設計の実際の一部として組み込む必要があり、設定フラグによって不要になるものではありません。40パッケージすべてのファイルを1つの巨大なプロンプトに連結する方法は、大多数の単純なケースに対してうまく機能していたパッケージごとのアプローチを完全に放棄し、対象を絞った修正を、モノレポが成長するにつれて実務上のコンテキスト上限を超えるリスクも伴う、より重く信頼性の低いアーキテクチャに置き換えてしまいます。

questions.context: Resuming a session after a teammate reverted a commit it depended on
questions.stem: An engineer paused a Claude Code session partway through building a new feature on top of a helper function a teammate had just merged. Overnight, that teammate reverted their own commit after discovering a bug in the helper function, removing it from the codebase entirely. The next day, the engineer resumes with `claude --resume <session-id>` and asks Claude to 'keep going.' Claude continues writing code that calls the now-nonexistent helper function, and the build fails. What is the most correct fix for this specific situation?

choices.text: Before asking Claude to continue, tell it explicitly in the resumed session that the helper function it was relying on was reverted (and why, if known), so its plan is grounded in the current state of the codebase rather than the state it last saw before pausing.

Treat this as proof that --resume is fundamentally unreliable for any feature work built on recently merged code, and adopt a blanket policy of never resuming a session that depended on a commit merged within the last week.

Resume with `claude --resume <session-id> --reconcile-vcs`, a flag that automatically diffs the current repository state against the state at pause time and updates the session's understanding of any reverted or changed commits before continuing.
Fork the session with fork_session to get a new session ID, then manually edit the forked session's stored transcript to remove every reference to the reverted helper function before resuming it.

questions.explanationEn: Telling the resumed session explicitly that the helper function was reverted grounds Claude's plan in the current codebase state instead of the stale state it last saw, which is the targeted, minimal fix for this specific, well-defined kind of drift. Adopting a blanket 'never resume after a recent merge' policy overcorrects: a single, clearly-communicable change like one reverted commit doesn't require discarding --resume's accumulated context and starting from nothing every time recent commits are involved. There is no `--reconcile-vcs` flag that automatically diffs repository state against pause-time state and updates the session's understanding; no such automatic version-control-reconciliation mechanism exists in Claude Code. fork_session is real for branching a new session from existing state, but manually hand-editing a session's stored transcript file is not a supported or reliable interface, and even if it worked, it wouldn't be the natural first-class way to communicate a specific, known change.
questions.explanationJa: 再開したセッションで『続けて』と頼む前に、頼りにしていたヘルパー関数がリバートされたこと(分かっていればその理由も)を明示的に伝えることで、Claudeの計画が一時停止前に最後に見た状態ではなく、コードベースの現在の状態に基づくようになります。これは、この種の明確に特定できるドリフトに対する、的を絞った最小限の修正です。『最近マージされたコードに依存していたセッションは絶対に再開しない』という一律の方針を採用する方法は行き過ぎであり、1つのリバートされたコミットのような明確に伝達可能な単一の変更のために、最近のコミットが関わるたびに--resumeが蓄積してきた文脈を捨てて毎回最初からやり直す必要はありません。`--reconcile-vcs`という、現在のリポジトリの状態を一時停止時点の状態と自動的に比較し、セッションの理解を更新するフラグは実在せず、Claude Codeにはそのような自動的なバージョン管理の照合の仕組みはありません。fork_sessionは既存の状態から新しいセッションを分岐させる実在の仕組みですが、保存されているトランスクリプトファイルを手動で編集することはサポートされた確実なインターフェースではなく、たとえ機能したとしても、特定の既知の変更を伝える本来の第一の方法ではありません。

questions.context: Overlapping calendar-scheduling tools
questions.stem: A scheduling assistant has two tools: `book_meeting(attendees, duration_minutes, earliest_start)`, described as 'Books a meeting,' and `create_event(title, start_time, end_time)`, described as 'Creates a calendar event.' In testing, the model frequently calls `create_event` with a guessed start_time and end_time when the user actually gave a duration and asked it to find the earliest available slot (something only `book_meeting` can do), and calls `book_meeting` with a single invented attendee when the user actually specified exact start and end times for a personal event with no other attendees. Both tools work correctly when called with appropriate inputs. What is the most direct fix?

choices.text: Keep both tools and their descriptions as they are, but add a `toolAffinity: "scheduling"` tag shared by both tool definitions so the SDK groups them together and biases tool_choice toward whichever of the two has been called most recently in the conversation.

Rewrite both tool descriptions to state clearly and non-overlappingly when each applies (e.g., 'book_meeting: use when the user wants the system to find an available time slot for one or more attendees, given a duration' vs. 'create_event: use when the user already knows and specifies the exact start and end time for a single calendar entry'), since tool descriptions are the model's primary signal for choosing between tools.

Remove create_event entirely and have book_meeting accept an optional exact start_time parameter that, when provided, causes it to skip the availability-finding logic and behave like a plain calendar-entry creator instead.

Keep both tools separate, but add a shared `disambiguationPrompt` field to both schemas that causes the SDK to pause and ask the user a clarifying question in plain text before either tool is called, on every single invocation regardless of how clear the request was.

questions.explanationEn: Tool descriptions are the model's primary signal for choosing between tools, so rewriting both to clearly and non-overlappingly state when each applies — availability-finding versus an already-specified exact time — directly resolves the ambiguity causing both misrouting patterns. A fabricated `toolAffinity` tag implying the SDK biases tool_choice toward whichever tool was called most recently is not a real mechanism, and conceptually it would make tool selection depend on conversational history rather than on which tool actually fits the current request. Collapsing both tools into one with an optional exact-time parameter is a plausible-sounding consolidation, but it conflates two genuinely different operations (finding a slot vs. recording a known one) into a single tool's branching behavior, trading the model's tool-selection problem for an internal-parameter-selection problem that's just as easy to get wrong. A fabricated `disambiguationPrompt` schema field that forces a clarifying question on every single call, even unambiguous ones, isn't a real SDK feature, and even conceptually it would needlessly interrupt clear-cut requests instead of fixing the actual cause of the ambiguous ones.
questions.explanationJa: ツールの説明はモデルがツールを選択する際の主要な手がかりであるため、両方の説明を、空き時間の検索なのか既に指定された正確な時刻なのか、どのような場合にそれぞれが該当するかを明確かつ重複なく述べるように書き直すことが、両方の誤ったルーティングパターンを引き起こしているあいまいさを直接解決します。両方のツール定義に`toolAffinity: "scheduling"`という架空のタグを共有させ、SDKがそれらをグループ化して直近に呼び出されたほうにtool_choiceを偏らせる、という仕組みは実在せず、概念的にも、ツール選択が実際の要求に合っているかどうかではなく会話履歴に依存してしまうことになります。両方のツールを1つに統合し、オプションの正確な開始時刻パラメータを持たせて指定されればスロット検索ロジックをスキップして単純なカレンダーエントリ作成のように振る舞わせる方法は、もっともらしい統合に見えますが、本質的に異なる2つの操作(空きスロットを探すことと、既知のものを記録すること)を1つのツールの分岐挙動に混ぜ合わせてしまい、モデルのツール選択の問題を、同じくらい間違えやすい内部パラメータ選択の問題に置き換えているだけです。両方のスキーマに架空の`disambiguationPrompt`フィールドを追加し、どれだけ明確なリクエストであっても呼び出しのたびに必ず明確化の質問で一時停止させる、という機能は実在するSDKの機能ではなく、概念的にも、曖昧なケースの実際の原因を修正する代わりに明確なリクエストまで不必要に中断させてしまいます。

questions.context: Payment-processing MCP server returning ambiguous charge failures
questions.stem: An MCP server's `charge_card` tool returns the plain string 'Charge failed' whenever (a) the card has insufficient funds, (b) the card is expired, or (c) the payment gateway itself is temporarily unreachable. A checkout agent currently reacts identically to every case: it tells the customer 'please try a different payment method.' For an expired card, that advice happens to work by accident (a different card sidesteps the issue), but for a gateway outage, switching cards accomplishes nothing since the gateway itself is down, and the agent keeps prompting the customer to retry with card after card during an outage that has nothing to do with any of them. What is the most correct fix to the MCP tool's error handling?

choices.text: Have the MCP server automatically wait 30 seconds and retry the charge once internally before returning any result, so a temporarily unreachable gateway has a chance to recover before the agent ever sees a failure.

Add an `errorConfidence: 0.0-1.0` field to the tool definition that the transport layer populates automatically based on how many times the same error string has been seen recently, letting the agent treat a low-confidence score as a signal the error is probably transient.

Return structured tool results with `isError: true` and a machine-readable `errorCategory` (e.g., 'business' for insufficient funds, 'validation' for an expired card, 'transient' for a gateway outage) plus an `isRetryable` flag, so the calling agent can branch its advice per case instead of telling every customer the same thing regardless of cause.

Change charge_card so that instead of returning an error string, it always returns a generic 'payment pending, please wait' response for every failure case, letting the agent avoid telling the customer anything went wrong at all.

questions.explanationEn: Structured results with isError, a machine-readable errorCategory distinguishing business, validation, and transient failures, and an isRetryable flag let the calling agent give the right advice per case — a different card for an expired one, waiting for a gateway outage — instead of one generic instruction that only accidentally helps some of the time. A single internal 30-second retry is a plausible partial mitigation for a brief outage specifically, but it does nothing for the insufficient-funds or expired-card cases, and a longer outage would still exhaust the one retry and fall back to the same undifferentiated failure the agent can't reason about. A fabricated `errorConfidence` field that the transport layer auto-populates from recent error-string frequency is not a real MCP mechanism, and even conceptually it's a poor proxy for the actual cause — a gateway outage and a wave of genuinely expired cards could both produce a repeated identical string. Always returning a vague 'payment pending' response for every failure, including real ones, actively hides that anything went wrong from the customer, which is worse than a generic error message, not better.
questions.explanationJa: `isError: true`と、機械可読な`errorCategory`(残高不足には'business'、期限切れカードには'validation'、ゲートウェイ障害には'transient'など)、さらに`isRetryable`フラグを含む構造化されたツール結果を返すことで、呼び出し元のエージェントがケースごとに適切な助言(期限切れなら別のカード、ゲートウェイ障害なら待機)を行えるようになり、たまたま一部のケースでしか役に立たない単一の汎用的な指示をあらゆる原因に対して同じように伝えなくて済みます。内部で30秒待ってから1回だけ自動的に再試行する方法は、短い障害に対しては一見有効な部分的緩和策に見えますが、残高不足や期限切れカードのケースには何の効果もなく、より長い障害であれば1回の再試行を使い果たして、結局エージェントが判断材料にできない同じ判別不能な失敗に戻ってしまいます。トランスポート層が直近のエラー文字列の頻度から自動的に値を設定する`errorConfidence`という架空のフィールドは実在するMCPの仕組みではなく、概念的にも実際の原因の代理指標として不十分です。ゲートウェイ障害と、本当に期限切れのカードが相次いだ場合の両方が、同じ繰り返しの文字列を生み出しかねません。あらゆる失敗(本物の失敗も含めて)に対して常に曖昧な『決済処理中、お待ちください』というレスポンスを返す方法は、何か問題が起きたことを顧客に対して積極的に隠してしまい、汎用的なエラーメッセージよりもむしろ悪化しています。

questions.context: Customer-facing chatbot forced to call a tool on every turn
questions.stem: A customer-facing chatbot was configured with `tool_choice` set to `{type: "any"}` for every turn, on the reasoning that 'the bot should always be doing something concrete, not just chatting.' It has access to a `search_knowledge_base` tool and an `escalate_to_agent` tool. During ordinary small talk ('thanks, that solved it!'), the bot now calls one of these tools anyway — sometimes escalating a satisfied customer to a human agent for no reason — because it's required to call some tool on every turn even when no tool call is actually warranted. What change most directly fixes this?

choices.text: Keep `tool_choice` set to `{type: "any"}` for every turn, but add 'do not call escalate_to_agent unless the customer explicitly asks for a human' to the system prompt, trusting the model to route to search_knowledge_base as a harmless default whenever no real tool call is warranted.

Set `tool_choice` to `{type: "throttled", max_calls_per_conversation: 3}` so the model is only forced to call a tool on the first three turns of any conversation, reverting to unforced behavior for the rest of the exchange.

Keep `tool_choice` set to `{type: "any"}` for every turn, but remove escalate_to_agent from the toolset entirely during ordinary conversation, and only add it back once the model has independently signaled distress in the customer's message.

Set `tool_choice` to `{type: "auto"}` for ordinary conversation turns, letting the model decide whether a tool call is warranted at all, and reserve a forced `{type: "any"}` or a specific forced tool only for turns where the application logic already knows a tool call is required.

questions.explanationEn: Setting tool_choice to "auto" for ordinary turns lets the model correctly decide that no tool call is warranted during small talk, while reserving a forced choice for turns where the application already knows a tool call is required — this directly removes the root cause, which is forcing a tool call on every single turn regardless of whether one makes sense. Keeping "any" for every turn and just telling the model not to escalate unless asked doesn't remove the forcing constraint — the model is still required to call some tool every turn, so it will still reach for search_knowledge_base (or something else) on pure small talk where no tool call at all is the correct response, not merely the correct tool choice among two options. A fabricated `{type: "throttled", max_calls_per_conversation: 3}` value is not a real tool_choice option — tool_choice accepts auto/any/tool(name)/none, not a call-count-limited variant — and even conceptually it would still force spurious calls on whichever early turns happen to be small talk. Conditionally removing escalate_to_agent from the toolset based on the model 'independently signaling distress' doesn't address the actual bug — search_knowledge_base alone is still forced on every ordinary turn under "any", so a satisfied customer's 'thanks, that solved it' would still trigger an unwarranted knowledge-base search.
questions.explanationJa: 通常の会話ターンではtool_choiceを"auto"に設定し、モデルにそもそもツール呼び出しが必要かどうかを自ら判断させ、強制的な`{type: "any"}`や特定のツールの強制は、アプリケーションのロジックが既にツール呼び出しが必要だと分かっているターンにのみ使うことが、根本原因(意味があるかどうかにかかわらず毎ターン強制的にツールを呼び出させていること)を直接取り除きます。毎ターン"any"のままにして、システムプロンプトに『顧客が明示的に人間を求めない限りescalate_to_agentを呼び出すな』と付け加える方法は、強制の制約そのものを取り除いていません。モデルは依然として毎ターン何らかのツールを呼び出す必要があるため、純粋な世間話に対してもsearch_knowledge_base(あるいは他の何か)を選んでしまい、これは2つの選択肢のうちどちらのツールを選ぶかという問題ではなく、そもそもツールを呼び出すべきでないという問題です。架空の`{type: "throttled", max_calls_per_conversation: 3}`という値は実在するtool_choiceのオプションではありません。tool_choiceはauto/any/tool(name)/noneを受け付けるものであり、呼び出し回数を制限するバリアントは存在せず、概念的にも会話の最初の数ターンがたまたま世間話であれば依然として不要な呼び出しを強制してしまいます。モデルが『独立して苦痛のシグナルを発した』ことに基づいて条件付きでescalate_to_agentをツールセットから取り除く方法は、実際のバグに対処していません。search_knowledge_base単体でも"any"の下では依然として毎通常ターン強制されているため、満足した顧客の『ありがとう、解決しました』という発言でも不要なナレッジベース検索が引き起こされてしまいます。

questions.context: Connecting Claude Code to an internal Slack-notification MCP server
questions.stem: A team wants every engineer's Claude Code session to be able to post build-status updates through an internal Slack-notification MCP server, where each engineer authenticates with their own personal Slack OAuth token, and the token must never be committed to the shared repository, while the server's command and connection arguments stay identical for the whole team. Which configuration approach correctly satisfies both requirements?

choices.text: Commit a project-level `.mcp.json` with the Slack MCP server's command and arguments, referencing the OAuth token as an environment-variable placeholder (e.g., `${SLACK_MCP_TOKEN}`) that Claude Code expands from each engineer's own shell environment at startup, rather than embedding any token value in the committed file.

Commit `.mcp.json` with one shared Slack bot token used by the whole team instead of individual OAuth tokens, since a single shared token still lets the server configuration and authentication live entirely in one committed file with nothing per-engineer to manage.

Have each engineer define the Slack MCP server independently in their own personal `~/.claude.json`, manually copying the exact same command and arguments block, so the shared project repository carries no MCP server configuration for Slack at all.

In `.mcp.json`, set `"auth": {"type": "oauthAutoRefresh"}` on the Slack MCP server entry so Claude Code automatically completes each engineer's OAuth flow and stores the resulting token without any environment variable being referenced.

questions.explanationEn: A shared, committed `.mcp.json` with identical command and arguments, but referencing the token through an environment-variable placeholder expanded from each engineer's own shell at startup, satisfies both constraints: one shared config, and no token value ever committed. Using a single shared bot token instead of individual OAuth tokens sidesteps the stated requirement rather than satisfying it — the team specifically wants each engineer authenticating with their own token, and a shared bot token also means every posted message is indistinguishable from any other engineer's, which the original per-engineer setup was presumably designed to avoid. Having each engineer hand-copy an identical server definition into their own personal `~/.claude.json` keeps tokens out of the repo, but abandons the single shared source of truth, requiring error-prone manual duplication instead of one committed configuration. Claude Code has no built-in `oauthAutoRefresh` auth type that completes an OAuth flow and manages tokens on its own — its documented secret-handling mechanism is environment-variable expansion from the shell, not an automatic OAuth-flow feature.
questions.explanationJa: 共有・コミットされた`.mcp.json`にコマンドと引数を記述し、トークンを起動時に各エンジニア自身のシェル環境から展開される環境変数のプレースホルダーとして参照することで、両方の制約(コマンドは全員同一、トークンは決してコミットしない)を満たせます。個々のOAuthトークンの代わりにチーム共有の単一のSlackボットトークンを使う方法は、要件を満たすのではなく回避しているにすぎません。チームは特に各エンジニアが自分自身のトークンで認証することを求めており、共有ボットトークンでは投稿されたメッセージがどのエンジニアのものか区別がつかなくなってしまい、これはおそらく元々のエンジニアごとの設定が避けようとしていたことです。各エンジニアが同一のサーバー定義を自分の個人用`~/.claude.json`に手作業でコピーする方法は、トークンをリポジトリ外に保つ点では機能しますが、単一の共有された設定源を放棄しており、1つのコミットされた設定の代わりにミスを誘発しやすい手作業の複製が必要になります。Claude CodeにはOAuthフローを完了しトークンを自動管理する組み込みの`oauthAutoRefresh`認証タイプは存在せず、文書化されているシークレット処理の仕組みはシェルからの環境変数展開であり、自動的なOAuthフロー機能ではありません。

questions.context: Creating many new per-service config files in one Claude Code session
questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to create 25 new, mostly-identical YAML config files (one per microservice) that don't exist yet, each differing only in a service name and port number. Claude Code's first approach uses the Bash tool to run a single shell heredoc command per file (`cat <<EOF > service-a.yaml ... EOF`, repeated 25 times), which works but produces content that's awkward to review in the conversation and error-prone to get the shell quoting right for. What is the correct, most direct way to create these 25 new files using the built-in tools?

choices.text: Use the Edit tool to create each file, since Edit is preferred over Write whenever the new file's content is templated from a shared pattern across multiple files, which is the case here since all 25 files share the same YAML structure.

Use the Write tool to create each new file directly with its intended YAML content as a normal string argument, once per file, since Write is the built-in tool designed specifically for creating new files with given content, without needing to route file creation through shell heredoc syntax and its quoting pitfalls.

Use the Write tool with a `batchCreate: true` option and a single call listing all 25 target paths and their respective content, since Write supports creating multiple files in one call when this flag is set, avoiding 25 separate tool calls.

Use the Bash tool with a `printf` command instead of a heredoc for each file, since `printf` is the preferred built-in-tool-adjacent approach over heredocs specifically for generating new file content, avoiding the quoting issues of `cat <<EOF`.

questions.explanationEn: Write is the built-in tool designed specifically for creating a new file with given content, so using it once per file directly supplies each YAML file's content as a normal string argument without routing through shell syntax and its quoting pitfalls at all. Edit is for modifying an existing file's content by replacing a matched anchor string — it isn't the tool for creating a file that doesn't exist yet, regardless of how templated or repetitive the content across files happens to be; that's a reason to write similar content efficiently, not a reason to prefer Edit's replace-in-existing-file semantics. Write has no `batchCreate` option or multi-file-in-one-call mode — it creates one file per call with the content given in that call; a fabricated flag claiming otherwise doesn't reflect how the tool actually works. Swapping `printf` for `cat <<EOF` still routes file creation through Bash and shell quoting rules either way — neither is the preferred built-in-tool path when Write accomplishes the same goal directly without any shell-quoting concerns at all.
questions.explanationJa: Writeは、与えられた内容で新しいファイルを作成するために特別に設計された組み込みツールであるため、ファイルごとに一度使うことで、シェル構文とその引用符の落とし穴をまったく経由することなく、各YAMLファイルの内容を通常の文字列引数として直接与えられます。Editは既存のファイルの内容を、一致したアンカー文字列を置き換えることで変更するためのツールであり、ファイル間で内容がどれだけテンプレート化・反復的であっても、まだ存在しないファイルを作成するためのツールではありません。それは似た内容を効率的に書く理由にはなっても、Editの『既存ファイル内で置換する』という意味論を優先する理由にはなりません。Writeには`batchCreate`というオプションや1回の呼び出しで複数ファイルを作成するモードは存在せず、1回の呼び出しにつき、その呼び出しで与えられた内容のファイルを1つ作成します。そうではないと主張する架空のフラグは、実際のツールの動作を反映していません。`cat <<EOF`の代わりに`printf`を使っても、いずれにせよファイル作成はBashとシェルの引用符ルールを経由することに変わりはなく、Writeが同じ目的をシェルの引用符の懸念なしに直接達成できる場合に推奨される組み込みツールの手順ではありません。

questions.context: Searching for a deprecated API usage across a monorepo with mixed casing
questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to find every call site of a deprecated function `fetchUserData` across a large monorepo before removing it, so all callers can be migrated to the replacement `fetchUserProfile`. A first Grep search for the literal string `fetchUserData` misses several call sites that use a re-exported alias imported as `FetchUserData` (capitalized) in a handful of older files, and also misses one file where the call is split across two lines due to a long argument list. What is the correct, most direct way to make sure the search is actually complete using the built-in tools?

choices.text: Run Grep with a `--semantic` flag so it understands that `FetchUserData` and `fetchUserData` refer to the same underlying function regardless of casing or import aliasing, and automatically expands the search to cover semantically equivalent references without needing case-insensitive or multiline options.

Rely on the original case-sensitive, single-line Grep search as sufficient, since JavaScript and TypeScript import aliases are case-normalized by the language itself before any static search tool sees the source text, so `FetchUserData` and `fetchUserData` would already appear identically to Grep.

Run Grep with case-insensitive matching enabled (to catch the `FetchUserData` alias) and, separately, run a multiline-aware Grep pass (or widen the search to account for line breaks) to catch the call site split across two lines, since a single case-sensitive, single-line pattern match is not guaranteed to find every real call site with a differently-cased alias or a wrapped argument list.

Switch entirely to the Bash tool and run `grep -r fetchUserData .` instead of the built-in Grep tool, since the Bash-invoked `grep` command supports case-insensitive and multiline matching by default with no additional flags needed, unlike the built-in Grep tool.

questions.explanationEn: Explicitly enabling case-insensitive matching catches the capitalized `FetchUserData` alias, and a multiline-aware pass (or widening the search) catches the call site split across two lines — a single case-sensitive, single-line pattern isn't guaranteed to find every real call site when casing and line-wrapping vary across the codebase. A fabricated `--semantic` flag implying Grep understands import aliasing and case-insensitive identity automatically is not a real capability — Grep matches text patterns, it doesn't perform semantic/static analysis of what a given identifier actually refers to in the language's import system. The claim that JavaScript/TypeScript normalizes import-alias casing before any tool sees the source text is factually wrong — source code is plain text on disk with whatever casing was actually typed, and a text-search tool sees exactly that text, casing included. Switching to Bash's `grep -r` doesn't gain case-insensitive or multiline behavior 'by default with no additional flags needed' — standard `grep` requires the same kind of explicit flags (`-i` for case-insensitivity, and different handling again for multiline matches) that the built-in Grep tool does; the claimed default-behavior difference between the two isn't accurate.
questions.explanationJa: 大文字小文字を区別しないマッチングを明示的に有効にすることで大文字化された`FetchUserData`エイリアスを捕捉でき、複数行対応のパス(または検索範囲を広げること)を別途行うことで2行に分割された呼び出し箇所を捕捉できます。単一の大文字小文字を区別する1行限定のパターンマッチでは、コードベース全体で表記や改行の仕方が異なる場合にすべての実際の呼び出し箇所を見つけられるとは限りません。Grepがインポートのエイリアシングや大文字小文字の同一性を自動的に理解するという架空の`--semantic`フラグは実在する機能ではありません。Grepはテキストパターンをマッチさせるものであり、ある識別子が言語のインポートシステムにおいて実際に何を指しているかについての意味的・静的解析を行うものではありません。JavaScript/TypeScriptがどのツールがソーステキストを見るよりも前にインポートエイリアスの大文字小文字を正規化するという主張は事実として誤りです。ソースコードはディスク上ではプレーンテキストであり、実際にタイプされた表記のままであり、テキスト検索ツールはまさにその表記を含むテキストをそのまま見ます。Bashの`grep -r`に切り替えても、『追加のフラグなしでデフォルトで』大文字小文字を区別しないマッチングや複数行対応が得られるわけではありません。標準の`grep`も組み込みのGrepツールと同様に、明示的なフラグ(大文字小文字を区別しないための`-i`、複数行マッチにはさらに別の扱い)を必要とし、両者の間にデフォルトの挙動の違いがあるという主張は正確ではありません。

questions.context: A hackathon-era model preference persisting in project memory
questions.stem: During a weekend hackathon, an engineer added 'use the fastest available model for all tasks, quality is not a priority right now' to the project's committed `./CLAUDE.md` so Claude Code would respond quickly during rapid prototyping. Two months later, the hackathon code was long deleted, but every engineer's Claude Code session on the main production repository (a completely different codebase that happens to share the same top-level `CLAUDE.md` after a repo merge) is still silently favoring speed over quality on serious production work, and nobody remembers why. What is the correct fix, and what does this reveal about where a note like this should have lived?

choices.text: Leave the instruction in place, but add a comment above it explaining it was originally written for a hackathon, so future engineers at least understand the historical context for why speed is being prioritized over quality.

Leave the instruction in place, since Claude Code automatically treats any model-tier preference stated in CLAUDE.md as expiring after 30 days from when it was first added, so it should have already stopped applying well before the two-month mark.

Move the instruction into the enterprise managed policy file, since enterprise policy is specifically intended for durable, organization-wide model-selection defaults that should persist reliably regardless of which specific repository or hackathon originated them.

Remove the stale model-preference instruction from the committed `./CLAUDE.md` now that the hackathon is long over; a temporary, situational preference like this shouldn't have gone into project memory (which every collaborator inherits indefinitely and which survived an unrelated repo merge) in the first place — it should have been stated directly in conversation for that weekend's sessions, or clearly scoped and dated if it had to be written down at all.

questions.explanationEn: Removing the stale instruction now that the hackathon is over directly fixes the problem, and the underlying lesson is that a temporary, situational preference shouldn't have gone into project memory at all — `./CLAUDE.md` is inherited by every collaborator indefinitely, with nothing marking it as tied to one weekend, so it silently outlived the hackathon and then survived an unrelated repo merge into production. Adding an explanatory comment doesn't fix anything — the instruction still silently deprioritizes quality on every serious production task, and understanding why it's there doesn't stop it from applying. There is no mechanism by which Claude Code automatically expires a model-tier preference in CLAUDE.md after 30 days or any other fixed period — CLAUDE.md content applies indefinitely until someone edits it, which is precisely why it's still active two months later. Enterprise managed policy is for durable, organization-wide settings that should persist reliably — moving a one-off hackathon preference there would make an already-misplaced temporary note even more durable and harder to remove, the opposite of the actual fix.
questions.explanationJa: ハッカソンが終わった今、古くなった指示を削除することが直接的な解決策であり、根本的な教訓は、一時的で状況依存の好みをそもそもプロジェクトメモリに置くべきではなかったということです。`./CLAUDE.md`はすべての共同作業者に無期限に継承され、それが特定の週末に紐づくものだと示す仕組みは何もないため、ハッカソンの後も気づかれないまま生き延び、その後無関係なリポジトリ統合を経て本番環境にまで持ち込まれてしまいました。説明的なコメントを追加する方法は何も解決しません。指示は依然としてあらゆる本格的な本番タスクで品質を黙って後回しにし続け、なぜそこにあるかを理解しても適用が止まるわけではありません。Claude CodeがCLAUDE.md内のモデル階層の好みを30日後や他の固定期間後に自動的に失効させる仕組みは存在せず、CLAUDE.mdの内容は誰かが編集するまで無期限に適用され続けます。まさにそれゆえに2か月後も依然として有効なのです。エンタープライズ管理ポリシーは、確実に持続すべき恒久的で組織全体の設定のためのものであり、その場限りのハッカソンの好みをそこに移動すれば、既に置き場所を誤っている一時的なメモがさらに恒久化し、削除しにくくなってしまい、実際の修正とは正反対です。

questions.context: A skill needing a required target-environment argument
questions.stem: A team builds a `/deploy-to` skill meant to be invoked as `/deploy-to staging` or `/deploy-to production`, where the target environment fundamentally changes what the skill does (different credentials, different confirmation requirements for production). Engineers keep invoking it as bare `/deploy-to` with no argument, and the skill's current behavior in that case is to guess an environment from ambiguous context, occasionally guessing production when staging was intended. The team wants the skill's documentation to clearly signal to engineers (and to Claude Code's own invocation-time display) that an argument is expected, and they also want the skill's own logic not to silently guess when no argument is given. Which combination of changes is correct?

choices.text: Set the skill's frontmatter `argument-hint` field to something like `<staging|production>` so engineers seeguidance on what argument is expected when the skill is listed or invoked, and separately add explicit logic within the skill's own instructions to refuse to proceed and ask for clarification whenever no environment argument was actually provided, rather than guessing.

Set the skill's frontmatter `argument-hint` field to `<staging|production>`, and rely on that field alone to also enforce that the skill cannot be invoked without a matching argument, since `argument-hint` both documents and validates required arguments in one mechanism.

Leave `argument-hint` unset, since it is purely a legacy field with no effect on modern skill invocation, and instead rely entirely on the skill's own instructions to ask for an environment whenever one isn't given.

Set `allowed-tools: <staging|production>` in the skill's frontmatter, since `allowed-tools` accepts either a list of tool names or a required-argument pattern depending on the skill's `context` setting, unifying tool-scoping and argument-validation in a single field.

questions.explanationEn: `argument-hint` is a display hint shown when the skill is listed or invoked, correctly signaling to engineers what argument is expected, but it doesn't itself enforce anything — separately adding explicit instructions telling the skill to refuse and ask for clarification when no argument is given is what actually stops the silent-guessing behavior, since that decision has to be made by the skill's own logic. Claiming `argument-hint` both documents and enforces required arguments in one mechanism overstates what the field does — it's a hint for display purposes, not a validation gate, so a skill relying on it alone for enforcement would still silently guess when invoked bare, exactly as before. `argument-hint` is a real, current frontmatter field, not a legacy one with no effect — dismissing it as non-functional and skipping it loses the documentation and invocation-time-guidance value it does provide, even though it doesn't perform validation on its own. `allowed-tools` controls which tools a skill may use; it does not have a dual mode that also accepts a required-argument pattern based on `context` — that's a fabricated overload of an existing field, not a real capability.
questions.explanationJa: `argument-hint`はスキルが一覧表示または呼び出された際に表示される表示用ヒントであり、エンジニアにどの引数が期待されているかを正しく伝えますが、それ自体は何も強制しません。引数が与えられなかった場合にスキルが拒否して明確化を求めるよう明示的な指示を別途追加することが、黙って推測してしまう挙動を実際に止める方法であり、その判断はスキル自身のロジックが行う必要があります。`argument-hint`が1つの仕組みで必須引数の文書化と強制の両方を行うという説明は、このフィールドが実際に行っていることを誇張しています。これは表示目的のヒントであり検証ゲートではないため、これだけに強制を頼るスキルは、引数なしで呼び出された場合、以前とまったく同じように黙って推測し続けてしまいます。`argument-hint`は無効化されたレガシーフィールドではなく実在する現行のフロントマターフィールドであり、機能しないものとして無視して省略すると、検証自体は行わないとしても提供される文書化と呼び出し時のガイダンスという価値を失ってしまいます。`allowed-tools`はスキルが使用できるツールを制御するものであり、`context`設定に応じて必須引数パターンも受け付けるという二重モードは存在しません。これは既存のフィールドの架空の多重定義であり、実在する機能ではありません。

questions.context: Different commit-message conventions for a public package versus internal tools
questions.stem: A monorepo has a `/packages/public-sdk` directory published as an open-source package (requiring Conventional Commits-style messages like `feat:`/`fix:` because they drive an automated changelog) and a `/tools/internal-scripts` directory of internal-only build scripts (where the team just wants plain, descriptive commit messages with no special prefix convention). The team wants Claude Code to automatically apply the Conventional Commits guidance only when committing changes under `/packages/public-sdk`, and the plain-message guidance only under `/tools/internal-scripts`, without an engineer needing to specify which convention applies each time. What is the correct mechanism, and why not a single top-level `CLAUDE.md` describing both?

choices.text: Write a single top-level `CLAUDE.md` describing both conventions, and set a `scope: inherited-strict` frontmatter key on the file so Claude Code parses which paragraph applies based on the most recently modified file's directory before generating any commit message.

Create two `.claude/rules/` files with YAML frontmatter glob paths scoping one to `packages/public-sdk/**` and the other to `tools/internal-scripts/**`, so each convention is conditionally loaded only for work in its matching directory — avoiding the risk of a single top-level file's two conventions bleeding together or one being misapplied to the wrong directory's commits.

Create the two `.claude/rules/` files as described, but omit the YAML frontmatter glob paths from both, since Claude Code infers each rule file's applicable directory automatically from the rule file's own filename if it's named to match a directory path.

Use a single directory-level `CLAUDE.md` placed at the monorepo root's immediate parent directory (one level above both `/packages` and `/tools`), since a `CLAUDE.md` one level up always takes precedence over anything inside `.claude/rules/` for commit-message conventions specifically.

questions.explanationEn: Two separate `.claude/rules/` files with glob-path frontmatter scoped to each directory conditionally load only the relevant commit-message convention for whatever's actually being committed, which is exactly the mechanism designed to prevent two different conventions from bleeding together or being misapplied to the wrong directory's commits. A fabricated `scope: inherited-strict` frontmatter key implying CLAUDE.md automatically detects which paragraph applies based on the most recently modified file's directory is not a real mechanism — CLAUDE.md doesn't have per-paragraph conditional parsing at all. `.claude/rules/` files are conditionally loaded based on the glob paths declared in their own frontmatter, not inferred automatically from a rule file's filename matching a directory path — omitting the glob paths removes the actual conditional-loading mechanism the team needs, leaving nothing to scope the rules by directory at all. There's no rule giving a `CLAUDE.md` one directory level above `/packages` and `/tools` automatic precedence over `.claude/rules/` specifically for commit-message conventions — that's a fabricated precedence rule, and even if such a file existed, it would apply uniformly rather than distinguishing between the two directories' different conventions, which is the actual requirement.
questions.explanationJa: `.claude/rules/`配下に、それぞれのディレクトリに対応するglobパスをフロントマターに指定した2つの別々のファイルを作成することで、実際にコミットされようとしているものに関連するコミットメッセージ規約だけが条件付きで読み込まれ、これはまさに2つの異なる規約が混ざり合ったり、間違ったディレクトリのコミットに誤って適用されたりするのを防ぐために設計された仕組みです。両方の規約を記述したトップレベルの`CLAUDE.md`1つに、`scope: inherited-strict`という架空のフロントマターキーを設定し、Claude Codeが直近に変更されたファイルのディレクトリに基づいてどの段落が適用されるかを解析する、という仕組みは実在せず、CLAUDE.mdには段落ごとの条件付き解析はそもそも存在しません。`.claude/rules/`のファイルは、それ自体のフロントマターで宣言されたglobパスに基づいて条件付きで読み込まれるものであり、ルールファイルのファイル名がディレクトリパスと一致することから自動的に推測されるものではありません。globパスを省略することは、チームが必要としている実際の条件付き読み込みの仕組みを取り除いてしまい、ディレクトリ別にルールをスコープする手段が何も残らなくなります。`/packages`と`/tools`の1つ上のディレクトリレベルの`CLAUDE.md`が、コミットメッセージ規約について`.claude/rules/`より自動的に優先されるというルールは存在せず、これは架空の優先順位ルールであり、たとえそのようなファイルが存在しても、2つのディレクトリの異なる規約を区別するのではなく一律に適用されてしまい、それはまさに要件が求めていることとは異なります。

questions.context: Choosing plan mode for consolidating overlapping caching layers versus bumping a version string
questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to 'consolidate our three overlapping caching layers (an in-memory LRU cache, a Redis cache, and a CDN edge cache) into a coherent caching strategy,' where several structurally different consolidation approaches exist with real tradeoffs around consistency, latency, and invalidation complexity. Separately, the same engineer asks Claude Code to 'bump the version string in package.json from 2.3.1 to 2.3.2.' Which use of plan mode best matches the guidance on when it adds value versus when it's unnecessary overhead?

choices.text: Set `planMode: "auto"` as a global Claude Code configuration so the tool itself automatically decides per task whether to invoke plan mode based on the number of files a task is likely to touch, removing the need for the engineer to reason about ambiguity versus mechanical simplicity at all.

Use plan mode for both tasks, since presenting an explicit plan before any file is touched is a strictly safer default regardless of a task's actual ambiguity, and the version bump's simplicity just means the plan itself will be short, not that plan mode should be skipped.

Use plan mode for the caching-consolidation task, since multiple structurally different approaches exist with genuine tradeoffs around consistency, latency, and invalidation worth surfacing before any architectural change is made; skip plan mode for the version bump and let Claude Code execute it directly, since it's a single, unambiguous value change with no competing approach.

Skip plan mode for the caching-consolidation task specifically because it involves infrastructure-adjacent components (Redis, CDN), and infrastructure-adjacent tasks are handled through a separate direct-execution workflow that bypasses plan mode by design; use plan mode for the version bump instead, since even a single-line change to a published package's version string carries external-facing risk.

questions.explanationEn: Plan mode adds real value for the caching-consolidation task because multiple structurally different approaches (in-memory, Redis, CDN — and how to unify them) exist with genuine tradeoffs worth surfacing before touching the architecture, while the version bump is a single, unambiguous value change with no competing approach, so executing it directly is appropriate. There is no `planMode: "auto"` global configuration that decides based on file count — and even if there were, file count isn't the actual criterion (a single-file change can still be highly ambiguous, and this pairing's own version bump is proof a change can be simple regardless of touching one file or many). Treating 'always plan first' as strictly safer regardless of ambiguity ignores the real overhead plan mode adds for genuinely unambiguous changes — it doesn't reduce risk on a version bump, it just adds an unnecessary approval step, and a 'short plan' for a trivial change is still an unneeded step, not a justified one. Claiming infrastructure-adjacent tasks are handled through a separate workflow that bypasses plan mode by design is fabricated, and reversing the pairing — skipping plan mode for the architecturally significant task while requiring it for the trivial one — applies the criterion backward in both directions.
questions.explanationJa: キャッシュ層統合のタスクでは、構造的に異なる複数のアプローチ(インメモリ、Redis、CDN、そしてそれらをどう統一するか)が存在し、アーキテクチャに手を付ける前に洗い出す価値のある本物のトレードオフ(整合性、レイテンシ、無効化の複雑さ)があるため、プランモードは実際の価値を発揮します。一方、バージョン番号の変更は単一の曖昧さのない値の変更で競合するアプローチが存在しないため、直接実行するのが適切です。タスクが触れそうなファイル数に基づいてツール自体がプランモードを呼び出すかどうかを自動的に判断する`planMode: "auto"`というグローバル設定は存在せず、たとえ存在したとしてもファイル数は実際の判断基準ではありません(単一ファイルの変更でも非常に曖昧なことがあり、この組み合わせのバージョン番号変更自体が、1つでも多くでもファイルに触れるかどうかにかかわらず変更が単純たりうることの証明です)。『常にまず計画する』ことを実際の曖昧さにかかわらず厳密により安全だと扱う方法は、本当に曖昧さのない変更に対してプランモードが加える実際のオーバーヘッドを無視しています。バージョン番号の変更のリスクを減らすわけではなく不要な承認ステップを追加するだけであり、些細な変更に対する『短いプラン』も、正当化されたステップではなく不要なステップのままです。インフラに近いタスクは設計上プランモードを迂回する別のワークフローで扱われるという主張は架空であり、組み合わせを逆にしてアーキテクチャ上重要なタスクではプランモードを省略し些細なタスクでは必須にする方法は、両方向で判断基準を逆に適用しています。

questions.context: Underspecified mailing-address normalization requirement
questions.stem: An operations manager asks Claude Code to 'clean up and standardize these mailing addresses' in a spreadsheet, without specifying whether street types should be abbreviated ('St' vs 'Street') or spelled out, how to handle apartment/unit numbers that appear in inconsistent positions, or what to do with addresses missing a ZIP code entirely. Claude Code's first attempt makes several judgment calls the manager didn't want once they review the output. Per established iterative-refinement practice, what is the most effective next step to converge on the right behavior efficiently?

choices.text: Set `interviewMode: true` in the session's configuration so Claude Code automatically pauses after its first attempt and generates a structured questionnaire covering every possible address-formatting ambiguity before any further work is attempted.

Produce three fully standardized versions of the entire spreadsheet, each using a different consistent formatting convention throughout, and hand all three to the manager to compare side by side and pick from without further discussion.

Before attempting anything further, research and adopt a formal postal-standards specification (such as a national addressing standard) in full, applying every one of its rules to the spreadsheet regardless of whether the manager's own preferences match that standard, so no clarifying questions are needed.

Interview the manager with a small number of concrete, example-driven questions grounded in real rows from the actual spreadsheet — e.g., show one address in two candidate formats (abbreviated vs. spelled-out street type) and ask which is wanted, and show one real row with a missing ZIP code asking how it should be handled — rather than guessing silently or asking one large, abstract question about 'formatting preferences' in general.

questions.explanationEn: A short, concrete-example-driven interview grounded in actual rows from the spreadsheet converges on the manager's real intent far faster than silently re-guessing or asking one large abstract question, which is the documented interview pattern for underspecified domains like this one. There is no `interviewMode` session configuration that automatically generates a structured questionnaire — no such built-in feature exists, and even conceptually, a questionnaire covering every possible ambiguity up front is the same over-engineering problem as writing an exhaustive specification, just relabeled as automatic. Producing three fully standardized versions of the whole spreadsheet multiplies effort without resolving the underlying ambiguity — the manager still has to reverse-engineer which convention they wanted from full outputs, and the next unspecified edge case (like the missing ZIP code) can still go wrong in all three versions. Adopting a formal postal standard wholesale without checking it against the manager's actual preferences is over-engineering for a domain the manager has explicitly not yet specified, and risks imposing rules that don't match what was actually wanted — a short interview against real rows resolves it faster and more accurately than an externally imposed standard.
questions.explanationJa: 実際のスプレッドシートの行に基づいた具体例駆動の短いインタビューは、無言のまま推測を繰り返したり、『フォーマットの好み』について一般的で抽象的な大きな質問を1つするよりも、はるかに速くマネージャーの実際の意図に収束します。これは、このような未規定の領域に対する文書化されたインタビューパターンです。構造化された質問票を自動的に生成する`interviewMode`というセッション設定は存在せず、そのような組み込み機能はなく、概念的にも、考えられるあらゆる曖昧さを事前に網羅する質問票は、単に自動化されたと言い換えられただけの、網羅的な仕様書を書くことと同じ過剰な作り込みの問題です。スプレッドシート全体の完全に標準化された3つのバージョンを作成し、3つすべてをマネージャーに比較・選択させてさらなる議論なしに済ませる方法は、実際の曖昧さを解決しないまま労力を増やすだけです。マネージャーは依然として完全な出力からどの規約を望んでいたかを逆算する必要があり、欠落したZIPコードのような次の未規定のエッジケースは3つのバージョンすべてで誤る可能性があります。マネージャーの実際の好みを確認せずに正式な郵便規格を丸ごと採用する方法は、マネージャー自身がまだ規定していないと明示している領域に対する過剰な作り込みであり、実際に望まれていたものと一致しないルールを押し付けてしまうリスクがあります。実際の行に基づく短いインタビューのほうが、外部から押し付けられた規格よりも速く、より正確に解決します。

questions.context: Automated release-note generation triggered by a git tag push in CI
questions.stem: Whenever a new version tag is pushed, a release-management team wants a CI job to invoke Claude Code, have it read the merged pull requests since the previous tag, and produce a structured, categorized release-notes draft (features, fixes, breaking changes) as a file in the repository for a human to review before publishing — with no one sitting at a terminal to drive it. Which combination of capabilities correctly supports this?

choices.text: Run Claude Code with `-p`/`--print` for non-interactive execution, giving it the tag range and instructions to gather the relevant merged-PR information via the prompt (using whatever tools/commands are needed to list commits and PRs between tags), and use `--output-format json` with a schema shaping the categorized release-notes structure so the CI script can reliably write it to a file for human review rather than parsing free-form prose.

Run Claude Code in its normal interactive mode inside the CI job whenever a tag is pushed, since `-p`/`--print` mode is designed only for single-turn informational queries and cannot run the git commands needed to gather merged-PR history between two tags.

Run Claude Code with `-p`/`--print --release-notes`, a dedicated flag that automatically detects the tag range from the triggering CI event and generates a categorized release-notes file without needing the tag range or instructions supplied via the prompt.

Run Claude Code with `-p`/`--print` and `--output-format text`, and have the CI script publish the release notes directly to the public changelog without human review, since structured categorization from the model is reliable enough on its own to skip a review step for this specific use case.

questions.explanationEn: `-p`/`--print` for non-interactive execution, combined with a schema-shaped `--output-format json` for a structured, categorized release-notes draft, gives the CI script a reliable file to write for human review rather than something that has to be parsed out of free-form prose. Describing `-p`/`--print` as limited to single-turn informational queries incapable of running commands is factually inverted — it's precisely the supported non-interactive mode for full agentic, tool-using CI runs, including running whatever git/PR-history commands are needed. There is no dedicated `--release-notes` flag that automatically detects a tag range from the CI event and generates output without any prompt-supplied instructions — that capability is fabricated; the tag range and task instructions need to be supplied explicitly via the prompt. Publishing release notes directly to a public changelog without human review contradicts the team's own stated requirement that a human review the draft before publishing, and skipping that step because the model's categorization is 'reliable enough' removes exactly the safeguard the team asked for, regardless of how good the categorization usually is.
questions.explanationJa: 非対話実行のための`-p`/`--print`と、構造化されたカテゴリ分けされたリリースノートのドラフトのためのスキーマ付き`--output-format json`を組み合わせることで、フリーフォームの散文から解析しなければならないものではなく、人間のレビュー用に書き出せる信頼できるファイルをCIスクリプトに提供できます。`-p`/`--print`が単一ターンの情報照会に限定されコマンドを実行できないという説明は事実として逆であり、これはまさにタグ間のgit/PR履歴を集めるために必要などのようなコマンドでも実行できる、完全にエージェント的でツールを使うCI実行のためにサポートされた非対話モードです。CIイベントからタグ範囲を自動検出しプロンプトによる指示なしに出力を生成する専用の`--release-notes`フラグは存在せず、この機能は架空のものです。タグ範囲とタスクの指示はプロンプトを通じて明示的に与える必要があります。人間のレビューなしにリリースノートを直接公開の変更履歴に公開する方法は、公開前に人間がドラフトをレビューするというチーム自身が明示した要件と矛盾しており、モデルの分類が『十分信頼できる』からといってそのステップを省略することは、その分類が通常どれだけ優れていようとも、まさにチームが求めていた安全策を取り除いてしまいます。

questions.context: Inbound support-email spam-detection agent over-flagging legitimate customers
questions.stem: An agent screens inbound support emails and flags any it judges 'could plausibly be spam or low-value' for a separate, lower-priority queue, guided by exactly that instruction. It currently routes an unacceptably high number of legitimate customer emails to the low-priority queue — terse one-line emails, emails with several links to the customer's own account pages, and emails in ALL CAPS from frustrated customers — alongside genuine spam. Which prompt change most directly reduces these false positives while preserving genuine spam detection?

choices.text: Keep the same instruction, but add 'weigh emotional tone carefully — angry-sounding emails are less likely to be spam' as additional guidance, trusting that a single heuristic about tone will correctly offset the other false-positive-prone signals like short length and links.

Replace 'could plausibly be spam or low-value' with an explicit, categorical description of what to flag (unsolicited promotional content, phishing-pattern links to external domains, mass-generic templated text with no reference to an actual account or issue) and an explicit description of what not to flag (terse messages, links to the company's own domain, all-caps text used for emphasis by a frustrated customer), rather than leaving the boundary to the model's sense of what 'could plausibly' be spam.

Keep the same instruction, and add a `spamConfidenceThreshold` field to the agent's configuration that the SDK automatically tunes over time based on how many of the agent's past flags a human reviewer subsequently overturned, without changing the instruction's actual wording.

Lower the model's temperature to 0 so its spam judgments become fully deterministic, which the team expects will also reduce the false-positive rate on short, link-containing, or all-caps legitimate emails.

questions.explanationEn: Replacing the vague 'could plausibly be spam or low-value' boundary with explicit categorical lists of what counts as genuine spam versus normal-but-superficially-similar legitimate patterns (short messages, own-domain links, emphatic capitalization) directly narrows the model's decision to a defined criterion instead of open-ended judgment, which is the documented fix for this class of false-positive problem. Adding a single heuristic about emotional tone doesn't address the other listed false-positive drivers (terseness, links, capitalization) at all, and treating one heuristic as sufficient to offset several independent sources of false positives overstates what a single added rule can fix. A fabricated `spamConfidenceThreshold` field that the SDK 'automatically tunes' based on overturned flags is not a real mechanism — no such adaptive-threshold auto-tuning exists, and it also doesn't change the underlying vague criteria being applied in the first place. Temperature 0 makes judgments deterministic, not more accurate — a temperature-0 model applying the same vague 'could plausibly be spam' criterion would just reproduce the same false positives on short, linked, or all-caps emails consistently every time rather than reducing them.
questions.explanationJa: 曖昧な『スパムや低価値である可能性がある』という基準を、本物のスパム(勧誘目的の迷惑メール、外部ドメインへのフィッシングパターンのリンク、実際のアカウントや問題への言及が一切ない大量生成されたテンプレート文)と、表面的には似ているが正常なパターン(短いメッセージ、自社ドメインへのリンク、苛立った顧客による強調としての全角大文字)の明示的・分類的な説明に置き換えることが、モデルの判断を無限定な裁量ではなく定義された基準に絞り込む直接的な修正であり、この種の誤検知問題に対する文書化された対処法です。感情のトーンについての単一のヒューリスティックを追加する方法は、リストアップされた他の誤検知の原因(簡潔さ、リンク、大文字)にはまったく対応しておらず、1つのヒューリスティックが複数の独立した誤検知の原因を相殺するのに十分だと考えるのは、追加された1つのルールが実際に修正できることを過大評価しています。SDKが取り消されたフラグに基づいて『自動的に調整する』という架空の`spamConfidenceThreshold`フィールドは実在する仕組みではなく、そのような適応的な閾値の自動調整は存在せず、そもそも適用されている曖昧な基準そのものも変わりません。temperatureを0にすることは判断を決定的にするだけで正確にするわけではなく、temperature0のモデルは同じ曖昧な『スパムの可能性がある』という基準を適用するだけで、短い・リンクを含む・全角大文字のメールに対する同じ誤検知を減らすのではなく毎回一貫して再現してしまいます。

questions.context: Ambiguous bug-severity classification in an incident-triage agent
questions.stem: An incident-triage agent classifies bug reports as 'sev1' (drop everything) or 'sev2' (normal priority). Zero-shot, it handles clear-cut cases well (a total outage is sev1; a minor UI misalignment is sev2) but is inconsistent on ambiguous ones — e.g., a report that a specific, non-default configuration option silently fails for a small subset of enterprise customers is sometimes classified sev1 and sometimes sev2 across otherwise-identical reruns. The team wants consistency specifically on this class of report, generalizing to differently-worded reports of the same underlying pattern (a real but narrow-blast-radius failure), not just memorizing this exact wording. What is the most appropriate fix?

choices.text: Add as many few-shot examples as can be pulled from the historical incident log, covering the widest possible range of exact report phrasings, on the theory that example volume alone drives consistency regardless of which specific cases the examples illustrate.

Remove the existing examples entirely and instead write a longer, more detailed zero-shot instruction defining 'sev1' and 'sev2' in the abstract with numeric thresholds for affected-user counts, since few-shot examples risk the model overfitting to the literal wording shown rather than generalizing the underlying severity pattern.

Add a small number of few-shot examples that specifically walk through the reasoning for ambiguous, narrow-blast-radius cases like this one — one example reasoned through to sev2 because the affected surface is small and non-default despite being a real failure, and a contrasting example that looks superficially similar but is actually sev1 (e.g., the same kind of narrow config option, but one that silently corrupts data rather than just failing visibly) — rather than only including clear-cut examples.

Add a `labelConsistencyScore` field to the classification output that the SDK computes automatically by comparing the current classification against the model's own classifications of similar past reports, and have the agent re-run its own reasoning until that score exceeds a fixed threshold.

questions.explanationEn: Targeted few-shot examples that walk through the reasoning for the specific ambiguous pattern (narrow blast radius but real failure), including a contrasting near-miss that resolves the other way (narrow but data-corrupting), teach the underlying reasoning pattern rather than exact wording, which is what generalizes to differently-worded reports of the same pattern. Adding a large volume of examples regardless of which cases they cover is a plausible 'more data helps' instinct, but if most of the added examples are still clear-cut cases, it doesn't address the specific ambiguous-pattern inconsistency and risks pattern-matching to literal phrasing instead of the underlying reasoning. Removing examples and relying on a longer abstract definition with numeric thresholds correctly names a real risk of few-shot prompting — overfitting to literal example wording — but draws the wrong conclusion, and a purely numeric threshold (like affected-user count) may not even capture what actually distinguishes this ambiguous class, since the scenario's key distinction is failure mode (visible vs. data-corrupting), not just count. A fabricated `labelConsistencyScore` that the SDK computes automatically by comparing against the model's own past classifications is not a real mechanism, and conceptually it's circular — using the model's own prior (possibly inconsistent) judgments as the yardstick for whether its current judgment is consistent doesn't introduce any independent signal.
questions.explanationJa: この種の曖昧で影響範囲の狭いケースについて、その推論過程を具体的に示す少数のfew-shot例(影響範囲が小さく非デフォルトであるため本物の失敗であってもsev2と推論する例と、表面的には似ているが実際にはsev1である対比例(同種の狭い設定オプションだが、目に見える形で失敗するのではなくデータを黙って破損させるもの))を、明確なケースの例だけでなく追加することが、正確な文言ではなく根底にある推論パターンを教え、同じパターンを異なる言い回しで表現している報告への一般化につながります。過去のインシデントログから引き出せる限り幅広い正確な文言のバリエーションを網羅する数多くのfew-shot例を追加し、どのケースを示しているかに関係なく例の量そのものが一貫性を高めると考える方法は、もっともらしい『データが多いほど良い』という発想に見えますが、追加された例の大半が依然として明確なケースであれば、特定の曖昧なパターンの不整合には対応できず、根底にある推論ではなく文字通りの言い回しにパターンマッチしてしまうリスクがあります。既存の例を完全に削除し、影響を受けるユーザー数の数値的な閾値を伴うより詳細な抽象的な定義に頼る方法は、few-shot例が示された例の文言そのものに過学習するという実在するリスクを正しく指摘していますが、そこから導かれる結論が誤っています。純粋に数値的な閾値(影響を受けるユーザー数など)は、このシナリオの本質的な区別が単なる件数ではなく失敗の様態(目に見えるか、データを破損させるか)であるため、この曖昧なクラスを実際に区別するものを捉えられない可能性さえあります。SDKがモデル自身の過去の分類と比較して自動的に計算するという架空の`labelConsistencyScore`は実在する仕組みではなく、概念的にも循環論法です。モデル自身の(一貫性がないかもしれない)過去の判断を、現在の判断が一貫しているかどうかの物差しとして使っても、独立したシグナルは何も導入されません。

questions.context: Order-confirmation email parsing hallucinating a delivery date
questions.stem: A logistics pipeline uses a forced tool_use call with a JSON schema to extract structured fields from order-confirmation emails (order_id, item_count, shipping_carrier, estimated_delivery_date). Roughly 12% of confirmation emails from certain carriers don't include an estimated delivery date at all (the carrier only sends that information in a later, separate notification), but the schema marks `estimated_delivery_date` as a required date field. The model reliably estimates a plausible near-future date in those cases based on typical shipping timelines — occasionally producing a specific date that doesn't match anything in the actual email and misleads a customer-service rep who trusts the field at face value. What schema-level change most directly reduces this specific hallucination?

choices.text: Keep `estimated_delivery_date` required and date-typed, but add a separate `date_source: "stated" | "estimated"` field so downstream code can tell which dates were directly present in the email versus inferred, while still requiring some date value in the main field either way.

Switch the whole extraction call's `tool_choice` from a forced tool call to `"auto"`, so the model can decline to call the extraction tool entirely for any email missing a delivery date, routing those emails to a human for full manual entry of all fields instead.

Add a `dateGroundingMode: "strict"` option to the JSON schema definition itself, which the underlying structured-output enforcement uses to reject any generated date value that cannot be located verbatim as a formatted date string somewhere in the source email text.

Make `estimated_delivery_date` a nullable field (accepting `null` in addition to a date value) rather than a required always-populated field, so the model has an explicit, schema-legal way to represent 'not stated in this email' instead of being forced to estimate a specific-looking date to satisfy a required field.

questions.explanationEn: Making `estimated_delivery_date` nullable gives the model an explicit, schema-legal way to represent 'not stated in this email' rather than being forced to produce a specific-looking estimated date to satisfy a required date field, which directly removes the forcing function behind this specific hallucination. Adding a `date_source` flag alongside a still-required date field is a plausible-sounding mitigation, but it doesn't remove the original forcing function — the model still has to invent some date for the required field either way, just now paired with a flag of uncertain reliability rather than an explicit 'unknown' state. Switching the entire call's `tool_choice` to `"auto"` so the model can skip extraction whenever the delivery date is missing discards the other well-extracted fields (order_id, item_count, shipping_carrier) along with the missing one, rather than fixing the field-level issue in isolation. A `dateGroundingMode` schema option that verifies a generated date against the literal source text is fabricated — JSON schemas constrain output shape and type, not semantic groundedness in a source document, and no such built-in verbatim-matching enforcement exists.
